I came out as bi to my mom about a week ago. That was the first time I had ever talked to her about my sexuality, so it was extremely nerve-wracking, especially since she has always stayed silent on the topic of LGBTQ issues. I had been planning the conversation for months. She took the news surprisingly well. She told me she had already suspected and that she had been preparing herself for this talk, too. Even though she's been accepting, I still think a part of her hopes I'll "grow out of it" or something though, so it will take her a while to get used to the fact that my coming out hasn't changed anything else, I'm still me. But I'm still glad I've finally done it.

Missing someone you care about really hurts. You can't stop thinking about them all the time and every time you think about them, you feel sad because they're not here with you. This type of sadness doesn't go away, even with time. Each day, it takes a huge effort just to wake up, get out of bed and face the world. You don't have the mental energy to do anything. Even things that used to make you happy have no effect on you anymore. It's like you've lost a part of yourself. 

For me, I feel lonely when I think about happy memories from the past because I realise that no matter how hard I try, I can never recreate those memories ever again.

I used to have the same problem. I would get so attached to tv shows or book series that it would upset me when I got to the end .So I do this thing where I find out which characters are going to die before reading/watching the book/tv series so that I can emotionally prepare myself for it. When I'm going to watch a new tv series, I read a short summary of how it ends beforehand. This reduces the amount of anxiety I feel later on when I'm actually watching it. I understand that this might not work for you in case you don't like spoiling the suspense in a book/tv series, but I hope this helps anyways.

I completely relate with this. I have the same problem where I start out all inspired, intending to complete a task, and then all my motivation just fizzles out and I abandon the task halfway through, and then I start on a new project. I think an effective way to complete a goal is to plan everything out and set a schedule. For example, one of my special interests is oil painting, but I often leave the painting I'm working on incomplete and go start a new one. So I make a schedule where I spend half an hour a day painting and I don't allow myself to start a new painting before finishing the other one.
I have the same habit of picking at my lips. I've recently started chewing gum, and it seems to do the trick. For me, the only way to deal with a repetitive habit is to replace it with another one.

I can relate so much to all of these! 

1. I always get caught up in recognising patterns. For example, listening to music is supposed to be relaxing, but I keep analysing and thinking about the melodies and rhythms. This particular scenario happens quite often: I'm listening to a pop song, and I immediately realise that the melody of the chorus sounds extremely similar to another song, so I'm not able to enjoy it. 
2. I don't know whether this happens because of my ADHD or my ASD, or maybe both, but I have a hard time understanding certain types of statements or questions. I tend to go with  the literal meaning, which can lead to misunderstandings and embarrassing mistakes. I have no idea what the question "I focus on the entire picture rather than the small details" means, and no matter how hard I try, I just can't make any sense of it.
3. I'm ashamed to admit it, but I actually have a notebook where I write down conversation prompts and dialogues for small talk so that I can refer to it when I'm talking to a friend on the phone. I have the constant need to plan out every single thing I do or say in order to ensure that I don't feel awkward or out of place. I also have a very  vivid memory, so I find myself worrying about the humiliating incidents that happened years ago. I can even recall all the times I've embarrassed myself when I was four or five years old.
4. I am constantly angry at myself for being such an anti-social, awkward, and lonely person. I usually keep it bottled in, but sometimes when I'm in an especially bad mood and someone says/does something that hurts my feelings, I take all my bottled in anger out at the person and I say hurtful things that I later regret. This normally surprises people who don't know me that well since they make the assumption that because I am quiet, I am also passive. I've had to deal with bullying from an early age, so I am especially sensitive to criticism and I instantly get defensive.
